title: India Just Let Four Chinese Power Equipment Firms Bid for Government Contracts. Five Years of Frozen Relations Are Thawing Fast.
excerpt: A Finance Ministry order gives TBEA Energy, Nanjing Electric India and two other Chinese-linked manufacturers a two-year exemption to compete for critical power tenders — the latest in a calibrated reset with Beijing.
body:
Five years after a deadly Himalayan border clash froze Chinese companies out of India's government contract market, New Delhi has opened the door — just a crack — to let them back in.

India's Ministry of Finance has granted four Chinese power equipment manufacturers with factories in India the right to participate in government tenders for critical power projects, according to a government order dated June 24 and reviewed by Reuters. The companies — TBEA Energy, Nanjing Electric India, New Northeast Electric India and Taikai Electric (India) — can now compete for state contracts without the political and security clearances that have blocked Chinese bidders since 2020.

The exemption is narrow and time-bound: two years, with explicit language that it should not be treated as a precedent for other companies. But in the context of India-China relations, even a narrow opening carries outsized significance.

## Why Now

India's power ministry had sought the exemption back in January, arguing that entities with manufacturing units in India should be allowed to participate in critical power projects regardless of their ownership structure. The reasoning is pragmatic: India is in the middle of an enormous expansion of its transmission network to support rising electricity demand and the integration of renewable energy sources.

The numbers tell the story. India has said it plans to add 97 gigawatts of coal capacity alone by 2035. About 48 to 50 GW of existing capacity already runs on Chinese equipment, installed before the 2020 restrictions. Domestic manufacturers have struggled to match Chinese timelines and pricing — Indian industry estimates suggest Chinese equipment can cut project costs by nearly half.

"Blocking Chinese imports would hurt India's manufacturing capability," one government official told Reuters when the broader relaxation was first reported in January.

## A Pattern of Calibrated Easing

This is not an isolated move. India has been quietly unwinding its China restrictions for months, driven by a combination of infrastructure urgency and a global trade realignment triggered by U.S. tariffs.

In recent months, India authorised state-run firms including Bharat Heavy Electricals and Steel Authority of India to procure specific critical equipment from China. BHEL received clearance for 21 types of components. The government also eased investment curbs on Chinese companies and resumed direct flights between the two countries.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited China last August for the first time in seven years, meeting President Xi Jinping to discuss improving bilateral ties. Since then, New Delhi has eased visa procedures for Chinese business professionals and begun examining broader relaxations on Chinese bidders across multiple sectors.

## The Geopolitical Calculus

The thaw sits at the intersection of three forces. First, India's infrastructure needs are real and urgent — the country cannot build its transmission network at the required pace without Chinese equipment. Second, the U.S.-China trade war has scrambled the global alignment, pushing India to hedge its relationships rather than pick a single camp. Third, China needs India's market. As the world's largest car market, fastest-growing energy consumer and a huge infrastructure spender, India offers Chinese manufacturers a critical growth outlet.

Tata Motors' recent deal to use Chinese automaker Chery's electric vehicle platform underscores the dynamic: Indian companies are importing Chinese technology while carefully avoiding deeper equity partnerships that would trigger political backlash.

## What Diaspora NRIs Should Watch

For the Indian diaspora, particularly those in the U.S. tech and energy sectors, the India-China reset has implications beyond geopolitics. NRIs working in energy infrastructure, renewable energy and power grid technology will see increased Chinese participation in Indian projects — which means both competition and potential collaboration opportunities.

Indian-American professionals in the clean energy space, many of whom bridge U.S. and Indian markets, should note that India's energy transition is pragmatically incorporating Chinese technology where it has a clear cost and timeline advantage, even as the broader strategic relationship remains guarded.

The two-year time limit on the exemption tells you everything about New Delhi's approach: use what you need, commit to nothing permanent, and keep the door open to pulling back if the political winds shift.
